name: Keyboard
subtitle: Piano & digital keys
description: Find your first notes, build two-hand confidence, and make the keys your own.
tuning: Middle C is C4 (MIDI 60). A4 = 440 Hz. Use headphones with the microphone.

lessons.title: Hello, middle C
lessons.goal: Find middle C and play four relaxed, even notes.
steps: Sit near the front of a stable seat, feet supported. Keep shoulders loose and forearms roughly level with the keys.
Find a group of two black keys near the centre. The white key just left of that pair is C; middle C is C4.
Place your right thumb on C4. Let your arm's weight press the key, then release. Play C four times, counting 1, 2, 3, 4 at 60 BPM.
Use the on-screen keyboard to hear C4, then try your own instrument. Stop if anything hurts.
lessons.tip: A curved hand is helpful, but do not force a shape. A relaxed wrist matters more than a perfect-looking hand.
lessons.pattern: C4 C4 C4 C4 · one note per beat
lessons.assessment: I found middle C and played four even notes without tension.

quiz.question: Where is C on the keyboard?
options: Just left of a group of two black keys
Just right of three black keys
quiz.explanation: Every C is the white key immediately left of a pair of black keys.

lessons.title: Five notes, five fingers
lessons.goal: Play C-D-E-F-G and back using right-hand fingers 1-2-3-4-5.
steps: Put your right thumb (1) on C4, index (2) on D4, middle (3) on E4, ring (4) on F4 and little finger (5) on G4.
At 60 BPM play C D E F G F E D C, one note per beat. Keep unused fingers near the keys instead of lifting high.
Repeat three times, then count aloud while you play. Slow to 40 BPM if the notes are uneven.
Listen for separate, clear notes. Let go of the previous note as you play the next, without gripping.
lessons.tip: Practise one accurate repetition before trying to go faster.
lessons.pattern: C D E F G F E D C · fingers 1 2 3 4 5 4 3 2 1
lessons.assessment: I played the five-note pattern three times with an even pulse.

quiz.question: Which number means your thumb in piano fingering?
quiz.explanation: For both hands, the thumb is 1 and the little finger is 5.

lessons.title: Make room for rhythm
lessons.goal: Distinguish one-beat quarter notes, two-beat half notes and silence.
steps: Set the metronome to 60 BPM and count four beats per bar. Clap once on every click for two bars.
Play C4 on beats 1 and 2, then hold E4 across beats 3 and 4. A quarter note lasts one beat; a half note lasts two in this exercise.
In the next bar, play G4 on 1, stay silent on 2, play E4 on 3 and C4 on 4. Keep counting during the rest.
Repeat both bars without adding a beat at the bar line. The reference below is a pitch guide; follow these counts for duration.
lessons.tip: Silence is part of the music, not a pause in your counting.
lessons.assessment: I kept counting through the held note and the rest.

quiz.question: In this 4/4 exercise, a half note lasts...
quiz.explanation: With the quarter note as the beat, a half note occupies two beats.

lessons.title: Your first C chord
lessons.goal: Play C major and hear its root, third and fifth.
steps: Place right-hand fingers 1, 3 and 5 on C4, E4 and G4. Play each note separately first.
Press C-E-G together, gently, and hold for four beats. Release all three together.
Repeat four times with a four-beat rest between chords. Check that every note speaks clearly.
Play C4 with the left hand while the right hand plays the chord. Start slowly and keep both wrists loose.
lessons.tip: The pitch reference plays chord tones in sequence. On your instrument, play them together.
lessons.pattern: C major = C E G · hold 4 beats, rest 4
lessons.assessment: I played all three chord tones clearly and released them together.

quiz.question: Which notes make C major?
quiz.explanation: C major uses the root C, major third E and perfect fifth G.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: little sunrise
lessons.goal: Play an original four-bar melody with a steady pulse.
steps: This original Playto melody uses C-D-E-G. Start at 50 BPM, right hand only.
Play | C D E G | E D C C | D E G E | D C C C |, one quarter note per beat. Use fingers 1-2-3-5 as needed.
Practise each bar twice, then join the four bars. Keep the beat through repeated notes.
For a challenge, hold left-hand C3 for each four-beat bar. Pass when you can play the whole piece twice without stopping; accuracy matters more than speed.
lessons.tip: A checkpoint is a chance to find what needs practice, not a penalty. Repeat freely.
lessons.pattern: | C D E G | E D C C | D E G E | D C C C |
lessons.assessment: I played Little Sunrise twice without stopping, with an even beat.

quiz.question: If a bar keeps going wrong, what helps most?
options: Practise that bar slowly, then reconnect it
quiz.explanation: Small, slow repetitions make the difficult movement easier to remember.

lessons.title: Cross the thumb: C major scale
lessons.goal: Play one octave of C major with smooth fingering.
steps: Right hand ascending: C D E F G A B C with fingers 1 2 3 1 2 3 4 5. After E, move the thumb gently under to F without twisting the wrist.
Descending use 5 4 3 2 1 3 2 1. Move the middle finger over the thumb from F to E.
At 40 BPM play one note per beat. Separate the crossing into E-F-G and G-F-E mini-patterns before joining the scale.
Play three even scales at 50 BPM, then try 60 only when the crossing is quiet and relaxed. Sing the notes as you go.
lessons.tip: C major has no sharps or flats. The half steps are E-F and B-C.
lessons.pattern: C D E F G A B C · 1 2 3 1 2 3 4 5 · reverse
lessons.assessment: I played the scale up and down with a relaxed thumb crossing.

quiz.question: The right-hand fingering ascending through C-D-E-F is...
quiz.explanation: The thumb crosses to F after fingers 1-2-3 on C-D-E.

lessons.title: Two hands, different jobs
lessons.goal: Keep left-hand whole notes underneath a right-hand melody.
steps: Learn each hand alone. Right hand: | C D E G | E D C C |. Left hand: C3 held for four beats in each bar.
At 40 BPM play both hands on beat 1, then keep the left hand down while the right hand continues on beats 2, 3 and 4.
Release the left-hand C just before the next bar, then begin both hands together again. Practise the bar line separately.
Repeat four bars without the left hand following every right-hand note. Add the metronome only when the coordination feels calm.
lessons.tip: You are teaching two independent motions. Short, slow loops beat long, tense repetitions.
lessons.pattern: RH: | C D E G | E D C C | · LH: | C3(4) | C3(4) |
lessons.assessment: I held the bass notes while the melody continued independently.

quiz.question: When the right hand changes on beat 2, the left hand should...
options: Move to the next bar early
quiz.explanation: Different note durations let the hands perform different musical roles.

lessons.title: Read the staff, hear the interval
lessons.goal: Read simple treble notes and recognise steps, thirds and fifths.
steps: Treble staff lines from bottom to top are E4 G4 B4 D5 F5; the spaces are F4 A4 C5 E5. Middle C4 sits on one ledger line below the staff.
Use the labelled pitch guide to find C4 E4 G4 A4 G4 E4. A step moves to the next letter, a third skips one letter, and a fifth spans five letter names.
Play C-E and C-G. Hum both notes and compare their distances. Try the ear-training tool below without looking at the keys.
Cover the guide labels and name the note positions. Then play the six-note phrase at 50 BPM, one quarter note per beat.
lessons.tip: Read the contour and intervals as well as letter names. That is faster than decoding every note separately.
lessons.pattern: C E G A G E · thirds, fifth and steps
lessons.assessment: I named the treble notes and heard the difference between a third and a fifth.

quiz.question: The bottom line of the treble staff is...
quiz.explanation: Treble lines are E G B D F; C4 is below on a ledger line.

lessons.title: C, F, G: the home chords
lessons.goal: Play I-IV-V-I in C major and hear the return home.
steps: Build C major (C E G), F major (F A C) and G major (G B D). Play each as separate notes before pressing it together.
Use comfortable right-hand fingers 1-3-5 for root-position chords, shifting the whole hand between shapes.
Play each chord for four beats at 50 BPM: C-F-G-C. Add the corresponding left-hand roots C3-F3-G3-C3.
Listen to how G feels unfinished and C feels settled. Use the backing tool to practise landing each chord on beat 1.
lessons.tip: In C major these chords are I, IV and V. Roman numerals describe their place in the scale.
lessons.assessment: I played C-F-G-C with the correct chord tones and a steady pulse.

quiz.question: The IV chord in C major is...
quiz.explanation: The fourth scale degree is F, so IV is F major.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: river steps
lessons.goal: Combine a melody, bass roots and clear phrasing in an original piece.
steps: Learn the original melody: | E G C5 G | F A C5 A | G B D5 B | E D C(2) |. All notes are quarters except the last C, a half note.
Use a left-hand root held for each bar: C3, F3, G3, C3. Practise the hands separately at 45 BPM.
Join one bar at a time. Breathe with the phrase and make the last C quieter than the highest D5.
Pass by playing the four bars twice at a comfortable 60 BPM, without losing the pulse or restarting at each chord change.
lessons.tip: The highest note can be the phrase's high point, not necessarily the loudest possible key strike.
lessons.pattern: | E G C5 G | F A C5 A | G B D5 B | E D C(2) |
lessons.assessment: I played River Steps twice with independent bass roots and shaped the ending.

quiz.question: How many beats does the last C fill here?
quiz.explanation: The final bar has E for one beat, D for one and C for two: four beats total.

lessons.title: Smooth chords with inversions
lessons.goal: Connect C-F-G-C with less hand movement using inversions.
steps: C major can be C E G, E G C, or G C E. The notes are the same; the lowest note determines the inversion.
Try right-hand C E G → C F A → B D G → C E G. F is second inversion, G is first inversion.
Play one chord per four beats at 50 BPM. Keep common notes near the same fingers; choose comfortable fingering without stretching.
Add left-hand roots C3 F3 G3 C3. Compare the smooth version with root-position chords and listen for the moving inner voices.
lessons.tip: An inversion changes the order, not the chord's identity. A C chord does not become E major just because E is lowest.
lessons.pattern: C E G → C F A → B D G → C E G
lessons.assessment: I connected the progression smoothly and named its inversions.

quiz.question: E-G-C is which chord and inversion?
quiz.explanation: E is the third of C major. Putting the third lowest creates first inversion.

lessons.title: Pedal, colour and release
lessons.goal: Use clean pedal changes and a deliberate dynamic phrase.
steps: On an acoustic/digital piano with a sustain pedal, play a C chord, then press the pedal just after the keys sound. Lift your hand and hear the sustain. Without a pedal, practise finger legato instead.
Change C to F: play F, release the pedal briefly to clear C, then press it again. Repeat slowly. The app's short reference tones do not simulate pedal behaviour.
Play C-F-G-C, four beats each, changing pedal after each chord attack. Listen for a clean harmony, not a cloudy wash.
Shape the progression from soft to moderately loud and back to soft. Use arm weight, not a stiff downward jab, and release tension after every phrase.
lessons.tip: Pedal follows listening. Use less in a resonant room, and never use it to hide unclear rhythm.
lessons.pattern: C → F → G → C · change pedal after each new chord
lessons.assessment: I cleared old harmonies with pedal changes, or used clean finger legato without a pedal.

quiz.question: Why briefly release the pedal at a chord change?
quiz.explanation: Clearing the previous notes prevents unwanted harmonic overlap.

lessons.title: Let the offbeat speak
lessons.goal: Maintain bass beats while the right hand plays on offbeats.
steps: Count 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & at 50 BPM. Clap only on the '&' after each beat, keeping the numbered beats silent.
Left hand plays C3 on beats 1 and 3. Right hand plays an E4-G4 dyad on each '&'. Practise each hand alone, then combine two beats at a time.
Repeat one bar four times. Keep the metronome at quarter-note beats; do not let the offbeat pull it faster.
Move the bass to F3 with right-hand F4-A4, then G3 with G4-B4, then back to C. Use light right-hand attacks and a steady low pulse.
lessons.tip: The reference is an equal-note pitch guide. The written '&' placements are what create syncopation.
lessons.pattern: LH on 1,3 · RH dyads on & after 1,2,3,4 · C/F/G/C
lessons.assessment: I kept bass notes on the beat while placing right-hand dyads off the beat.

quiz.question: An '&' in 1 & 2 & means...
options: The eighth-note halfway between numbered beats
quiz.explanation: Each quarter-note beat is divided into two equal eighth notes.

lessons.title: Improvise a conversation
lessons.goal: Create and develop a short motif over a chord progression.
steps: Use C major pentatonic: C D E G A. Play the five notes and notice there are no half steps within this set.
Over the C-F-G-C backing, invent a two-beat idea using only C D E. Repeat it, then change its last note. Leave a full beat of silence between answers.
On F bars, aim for A or C; on G bars, aim for G or D; on the final C bar, settle on C or E. These tones connect the idea to the chord.
Record the motif on paper using letter names and beat counts. Perform three variations while keeping the same opening rhythm. Try identifying intervals in the ear tool before playing them.
lessons.tip: Improvisation is making choices, not filling every space. A recognisable idea is more memorable than a fast scale.
lessons.pattern: C D E G A · motif → repeat → vary → leave space
lessons.assessment: I played three motif variations and landed on chord tones at the changes.

quiz.question: Which set is C major pentatonic?
quiz.explanation: The major pentatonic uses scale degrees 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6.

lessons.title: Level test: your own arrangement
lessons.goal: Arrange an original eight-bar piece using melody, harmony and expression.
steps: Use two cycles of C-F-G-C, one four-beat bar each. For the first cycle play River Steps with left-hand roots and smooth right-hand melody at 65 BPM.
For the second cycle replace the melody with your own pentatonic motif. Use inversions to reduce movement, and add a brief offbeat response only if you can keep time.
Choose a dynamic high point in bar 7 and a quiet, clear ending in bar 8. Add clean pedal changes if available.

Pass with two uninterrupted takes: clear chord changes, independent hands, audible phrase shape, and an ending on C harmony. Write one thing to improve next; do not increase tempo until both takes feel controlled.
lessons.tip: Advanced work here is an introduction to arranging and independence, not a claim of concert-pianist mastery. Revisit techniques with a teacher.
lessons.pattern: 8 bars: C F G C | C F G C · melody, then original variation
lessons.assessment: I performed two complete arrangements with clean harmony, steady time and intentional expression.

quiz.question: Which makes this arrangement most musical?
options: Clear time, connected harmony, and intentional phrasing
quiz.explanation: A controlled musical idea is more important than density or speed.
